candidate.answerReason: On the feasible interval 0<x<12, the area increases until x=6 and decreases afterwards, so its unique maximum occurs at x=6 meters.

methods.label: Use the derivative's sign
methods.explanation: The sign of the area derivative tells us where the area increases or decreases. For a genuine rectangle, \(0<x<12\). \(S=x(24-2x)=24x-2x^2\), \(S'=24-4x=0\), so \(x=6\). Since \(S'(x)>0\) for \(0<x<6\) and \(S'(x)<0\) for \(6<x<12\), the area increases up to \(6\) and decreases afterwards. Hence its greatest value occurs when \(x=6\) meters.
methods.levelReason: The repaired existing main method uses polynomial differentiation and derivative-sign monotonicity, both within Elective mathematics II.

methods.label: Complete the square
methods.explanation:
Both side lengths must be positive, so \(0<x<12\). Writing the area as a constant minus a square makes its upper bound visible:
\[
S=x(24-2x)=72-2(x-6)^2\le72.
\]
Equality holds exactly when \(x=6\), which lies in the allowed interval. Thus the area is greatest when \(x=6\) meters.
methods.levelReason: This distinct alternative uses earlier school algebra and requires fewer prerequisites than the derivative method.
